claim: Low oxygen levels increase effector differentiation of T cells, upregulating molecules such as CD25, EOMES, T-bet, TOX, granzyme B (GZMB), and interferon-γ (IFN-γ).
source: Low oxygen levels increased effector differentiation of T cells, upregulating molecules such as the IL-2 receptor alpha subunit CD25, the transcription factors EOMES, T-bet, and TOX, and the effector proteins granzyme B (GZMB) and interferon-γ (IFN-γ) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing increased expression of these markers in T cells cultured at low oxygen tensions, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: T cells cultured at 1% O2 have increased expression of inhibitory receptors and impaired clonal expansion.
source: T cells cultured at 1% O2 have increased expression of inhibitory receptors and impaired clonal expansion (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced cell expansion and increased inhibitory receptor expression in 1% O2 conditions, as shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: HIF-1α protein expression increases after T cell activation and peaks within 12 hr in all oxygen tensions tested.
source: In all oxygen tensions tested, HIF-1α protein expression increased after T cell activation and peaked within 12 hr.
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis of HIF-1α protein levels at different time points after T cell activation shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Exposure to 1% O2 results in the greatest accumulation of HIF-1α during 3 days of culture.
source: Exposure to 1% O2 resulted in the greatest accumulation of HIF-1α during the 3 d of culture (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing higher HIF-1α protein levels in 1% O2 conditions compared to 5% and 21% O2, as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: HIF-2α protein is mostly found in the cytoplasmic protein fraction after T cell activation.
source: HIF-2α protein was also increased in T cells following activation, but was mostly found in the cytoplasmic protein fraction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), as previously seen (Park et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis of nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, and by citation to Park et al., 2003.

claim: Deletion of HIF-1α, but not HIF-2α, abrogates hypoxia-driven increases in GZMB.
source: This is consistent with data showing that deletion of HIF-1α, but not HIF-2α, abrogates hypoxia-driven increases in GZMB (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and other activation markers, and impairs antitumour T cell function (Palazon et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from HIF-1α and HIF-2α knockout T cells shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, and by citation to Palazon et al., 2017.

claim: FG-4592 treatment increases the expression of GZMB and IFN-γ in OT-I cells.
source: At the selected concentration (50 µM), FG-4592 increased the expression of the effector molecules GZMB and IFN-γ and had a reduced impact on cell expansion when compared to 1% O2, which is relevant for an ex vivo protocol of T cell expansion (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing increased GZMB and IFN-γ expression in FG-4592-treated OT-I cells, as shown in Figure 1F.

claim: OT-I cells grown in 1% O2 show increased antigen-specific cytotoxicity against B16F10 melanoma tumour cells expressing OVA peptide.
source: OT-I cells grown in 1% O2 showed increased antigen-specific cytotoxicity against B16F10 melanoma tumour cells expressing OVA peptide when compared to wild-type CD8+ T cells grown at 21% O2 (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: Supported by in vitro cytotoxicity assay data showing lower EC50 values for 1% O2-conditioned OT-I cells, as shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: Increased cytotoxicity in 1% O2-conditioned T cells occurs when assays are conducted at 1% O2, 5% O2, or 21% O2.
source: This increased cytotoxicity occurred when assays were conducted at 1% O2, 5% O2, or 21% O2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by cytotoxicity assay data performed at different oxygen tensions, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: 5% O2 conditioning for 3 days did not impact OT-I cell function under the experimental conditions in vitro.
source: Despite belonging to the physiological oxygen range at which cells are exposed to in vivo, 5% O2 did not impact OT-I cell function under our experimental conditions in vitro, nor did the 3 d treatment with FG-4592 (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by cytotoxicity assay data showing no significant difference in EC50 values for 5% O2 or FG-4592-treated cells compared to 21% O2 controls, as shown in Figure 1H.

claim: A trade-off relationship exists between CD8+ T cell proliferation and effector function when induced by low oxygen tensions and increased HIF signalling.
source: Increased cytotoxicity in these populations (illustrated by lower EC50 values) was accompanied by decreased cell numbers on day 3 (Figure 1I), highlighting that a trade-off relationship exists between CD8+ T cell proliferation and effector function when these are induced by low oxygen tensions and increased HIF signalling.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between cell counts and EC50 values shown in Figure 1I, demonstrating inverse relationship between proliferation and cytotoxicity.

claim: Culturing OT-I CD8+ T cells in 1% O2 for 3 days ex vivo markedly improves their expansion in peripheral blood 7 days after adoptive cell transfer.
source: Culturing of OT-I CD8+ T cells in 1% O2 ex vivo markedly improved expansion in peripheral blood when the numbers of transferred cells were assayed at 7 d after ACT (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis of peripheral blood showing increased OT-I cell numbers in the 1% O2 group, as shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: T cells cultured in 1% O2 have a higher proportion of terminally differentiated CD62L-CD44+ cells 7 days after adoptive cell transfer.
source: T cells cultured in 1%O2 additionally had a higher proportion of terminally differentiated CD62L-CD44+ cells 7 d after ACT (Figure 2D), following their pattern of increased expression of CD44 and reduced levels of CD62L observed in vitro (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis of peripheral blood showing increased CD62L-CD44+ cells in the 1% O2 group, as shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Adoptive transfer of FG-4592- or 1% O2-treated OT-I T cells initially decreases tumour burdens compared to 21% O2-treated cells.
source: When compared to animals receiving WT OT-I cells grown at 21% O2, adoptive transfer of FG-4592- or 1% O2-treated OT-I T cells was found to initially decrease tumour burdens (Figure 2E and F); while FG-4592-treated cells significantly extended animal survival (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by tumour growth measurements and survival analysis shown in Figure 2E, F, and G.

claim: FG-4592-treated OT-I cells significantly extend animal survival in a B16-OVA tumour model.
source: When compared to animals receiving WT OT-I cells grown at 21% O2, adoptive transfer of FG-4592- or 1% O2-treated OT-I T cells was found to initially decrease tumour burdens (Figure 2E and F); while FG-4592-treated cells significantly extended animal survival (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by survival curve analysis showing statistically significant improvement in survival for FG-4592-treated group, as shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Transduction of human CD8+ T cells with VHL-targeted shRNA reduces VHL expression by approximately 30%.
source: Transduction of human CD8+ T cells with VHL-targeted shRNA (shVHL) using an engineered CAR vector reduced VHL expression by approximately 30% (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D); this was sufficient to detectably increase HIF levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis showing reduced VHL protein levels in shVHL-transduced cells, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: VHL silencing by approximately 30% is sufficient to detectably increase HIF levels in human CD8+ T cells.
source: Transduction of human CD8+ T cells with VHL-targeted shRNA (shVHL) using an engineered CAR vector reduced VHL expression by approximately 30% (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D); this was sufficient to detectably increase HIF levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis showing increased HIF-1α protein levels in shVHL-transduced cells, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: FG-4592 treatment for 7 days reduces cytotoxicity of CAR-T cells in vitro.
source: In vitro, while FG-4592 treatment reduced cytotoxicity of CAR-T cells, shVHL-expressing CAR-T cells showed enhanced tumour cell killing capacity in 21 and 1% O2 (Figure 3D and E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and I).
evidence: Supported by in vitro cytotoxicity assay data showing higher EC50 values for FG-4592-treated CAR-T cells, as shown in Figure 3D.

claim: shVHL-expressing CAR-T cells show enhanced tumour cell killing capacity in vitro at 21% and 1% O2.
source: In vitro, while FG-4592 treatment reduced cytotoxicity of CAR-T cells, shVHL-expressing CAR-T cells showed enhanced tumour cell killing capacity in 21 and 1% O2 (Figure 3D and E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and I).
evidence: Supported by in vitro cytotoxicity assay data showing lower EC50 values for shVHL-expressing CAR-T cells, as shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Short-term exposure to FG-4592 for 1 or 3 days does not impair antitumour T cell function.
source: In contrast to 7 d treatments, short-term exposure to FG-4592 for 1 or 3 d did not impair antitumour T cell function (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J and K), implying that the timing of HIF expression during T cell activation is crucial for regulation of cytotoxicity.
evidence: Supported by cytotoxicity assay data showing no impairment in function with short-term FG-4592 treatment, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J and K.

claim: The timing of HIF expression during T cell activation is crucial for regulation of cytotoxicity.
source: In contrast to 7 d treatments, short-term exposure to FG-4592 for 1 or 3 d did not impair antitumour T cell function (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J and K), implying that the timing of HIF expression during T cell activation is crucial for regulation of cytotoxicity.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of short-term versus long-term FG-4592 treatment on T cell cytotoxicity.

claim: FG-4592-treated CAR-T cells expand to a greater extent in the blood after adoptive cell transfer compared to DMSO-treated control T cells.
source: After ACT was delivered to recipient animals, FG-treated CAR-T cells expanded to a greater extent in the blood relative to DMSO-treated control T cells (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis of peripheral blood showing increased CAR-T cell numbers in the FG-4592 group, as shown in Figure 3G.

claim: FG-4592-treated CAR-T cells delayed tumour growth in 50% of animals compared to 9% in the control T cell group.
source: Tumour growth analyses showed that, relative to animals not receiving CAR-T cells, FG-4592-treated CAR-T cells delayed tumour growth in 50% of the animals compared to 9% of the animals in the control T cell group (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by tumour growth curve analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: VHL-silenced HER2-CAR-T cells decrease tumour growth significantly and improve animal survival relative to NTC-expressing CAR-T cells.
source: However, VHL-silenced HER2-CAR-T cells were able to decrease tumour growth significantly, and an improved animal survival relative to NTC-expressing CAR-T cells was seen, clearing tumours in 2 of the 11 animals analysed (Figure 3K and L).
evidence: Supported by tumour growth measurements and survival analysis shown in Figure 3K and L.

claim: Longer periods spent at 1% O2 correlate with the strongest reduction in cell numbers when compared to 21% O2-grown cells.
source: Longer periods spent at 1% O2 correlated with the strongest reduction in cell numbers when compared to 21% O2-grown cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by cell count data showing progressive decrease in cell numbers with longer exposure to 1% O2, as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The expression of differentiation markers elicited by 1, 3, and 7 days of 1% O2 conditioning is remarkably similar, although the magnitude of differential expression increases with longer exposure.
source: However, the expression of differentiation markers elicited by 1, 3, and 7 d of 1% O2 conditioning was remarkably similar, although the magnitude of differential expression increased with longer exposure to 1% O2 (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis of differentiation markers at different durations of 1% O2 exposure, as shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Incubation in low oxygen conditions (1 or 5% O2) during the last 3 days of culture has little effect on T cell differentiation.
source: On the other hand, incubation in low oxygen conditions (1 or 5% O2) during the last 3 d of culture had little effect (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F), despite leading to the highest levels of HIF-1α on day 7 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis showing minimal changes in differentiation markers when low oxygen exposure occurs in the last 3 days, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: A single day of 1% O2 conditioning during T cell activation leads to increased baseline glycolytic rate and glycolytic reserve.
source: In fact, a single day of 1% O2 conditioning, occurring at the time of activation, followed by 6 d of 21% O2 culture, was sufficient to elicit a classical hypoxia/HIF-driven metabolic adaptation in T cells as characterised by an increased baseline glycolytic rate and glycolytic reserve (Figure 4D; Papandreou et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse analysis showing increased ECAR and glycolytic reserve in 1% 1d cells, as shown in Figure 4D, and by citation to Papandreou et al., 2006.

claim: Short-term exposure to 1% O2 at the time of activation leads to increased baseline oxygen consumption rates, increased spare respiratory capacity, and ATP production.
source: This short-term exposure to hypoxia at the time of activation also led to increased baseline oxygen consumption rates, increased spare respiratory capacity, and ATP production (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse analysis showing increased OCR, spare respiratory capacity, and ATP production in 1% 1d cells, as shown in Figure 4E.

claim: 1% O2 conditioning for 1 day leads to increased mitochondrial DNA copy number.
source: The change in oxygen consumption rates was accompanied by both an increased mitochondrial DNA copy number (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K) and increased Mitotracker (indicating increased mitochondrial mass) and increased TMRM staining (indicating a shift in mitochondrial membrane potential) (Figure 4F) when compared to cells continuously grown in 21% O2, as measured at 7 d following initial activation.
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis of mitochondrial DNA content shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1K.

claim: 1% O2 conditioning for 1 day leads to increased Mitotracker staining, indicating increased mitochondrial mass.
source: The change in oxygen consumption rates was accompanied by both an increased mitochondrial DNA copy number (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K) and increased Mitotracker (indicating increased mitochondrial mass) and increased TMRM staining (indicating a shift in mitochondrial membrane potential) (Figure 4F) when compared to cells continuously grown in 21% O2, as measured at 7 d following initial activation.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis of Mitotracker staining shown in Figure 4F.

claim: 1% O2 conditioning for 1 day leads to increased TMRM staining, indicating a shift in mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: The change in oxygen consumption rates was accompanied by both an increased mitochondrial DNA copy number (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K) and increased Mitotracker (indicating increased mitochondrial mass) and increased TMRM staining (indicating a shift in mitochondrial membrane potential) (Figure 4F) when compared to cells continuously grown in 21% O2, as measured at 7 d following initial activation.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis of TMRM staining shown in Figure 4F.

claim: 1% 1d-treated CD8+ T cells accumulate acylcarnitines including laurylcarninite, oleoylcarnitine, palmitoylcarninite, and mysteroylcarnitine.
source: Analysis of metabolites feeding the TCA cycle showed that 1% 1 d-treated CD8+ T cells accumulate acylcarnitines (namely, laurylcarninite, oleoylcarnitine, palmitoylcarninite, and mysteroylcarnitine) (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis of metabolites shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The accumulation of acylcarnitines suggests that increased oxygen consumption rates in hypoxia-conditioned T cells may result from increased contribution of lipids to oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Acylcarnitines are intermediates in fatty acid metabolism that are involved in the transport of fatty acids into the mitochondria for energy production (McCoin et al., 2015). Their accumulation suggests that the increased oxygen consumption rates displayed by hypoxia-conditioned T cells may result from an increased contribution of these lipids to oxidative phosphorylation (Figure 4E).
evidence: Inferred from the known role of acylcarnitines in fatty acid metabolism (cited to McCoin et al., 2015) and the observed accumulation of these metabolites in hypoxia-conditioned cells.

claim: Exposure to 1% O2 during T cell activation for a single day leads to altered levels of specific post-translational histone modifications after 6 days of conditioning in ambient oxygen.
source: It has been previously established that hypoxia rapidly modulates histone methylation and chromatin structure (Batie et al., 2019; Chakraborty et al., 2019). In line with this, our study reveals that even after 6 d of conditioning in ambient oxygen levels, exposure to 1% O2 during T cell activation for a single day led to altered levels of specific post-translational histone modifications (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis of histone modifications shown in Figure 4H, and by citations to Batie et al., 2019 and Chakraborty et al., 2019.

claim: The broad reduction in histone methylation could result from decreased methionine levels.
source: The broad reduction in histone methylation could result from decreased methionine levels (Figure 4I).
evidence: Inferred from the observed reduction in histone methylation and decreased methionine levels shown in Figure 4I, and from the known role of methionine in methylation reactions.

claim: 5-methylthioadenosine (MTA) is reduced by short, low oxygen conditioning of T cells during activation.
source: While SAM levels were under the detection limit, analysis of metabolites involved in the methionine cycle showed that 5-methylthioadenosine (MTA) is reduced by short, low oxygen conditioning of T cells during activation (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis of metabolites involved in the methionine cycle shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Nuclear translocation of NFAT1 is reduced by 1% O2 and PHD inhibition.
source: Nuclear translocation of NFAT1 was reduced by 1% O2 and PHD inhibition, whereas the levels of nuclear factor kappa B (NFkB) were only reduced in the nuclear fraction of 1% O2 activated T cells.
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis of nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Nuclear levels of NFkB are only reduced in 1% O2 activated T cells, not by PHD inhibition.
source: Nuclear translocation of NFAT1 was reduced by 1% O2 and PHD inhibition, whereas the levels of nuclear factor kappa B (NFkB) were only reduced in the nuclear fraction of 1% O2 activated T cells.
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis of nuclear fractions shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Levels of PGC-1α are increased by T cell activation in 1% O2.
source: Levels of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α, a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis; Liang and Ward, 2006) and c-Myc (a primary mediator of glycolysis in T cells; Wang et al., 2011) were respectively increased and decreased by T cell activation in 1% O2 (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis showing increased PGC-1α protein levels in 1% O2 activated T cells, as shown in Figure 5B, and by citation to Liang and Ward, 2006.

claim: Levels of c-Myc are decreased by T cell activation in 1% O2.
source: Levels of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α, a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis; Liang and Ward, 2006) and c-Myc (a primary mediator of glycolysis in T cells; Wang et al., 2011) were respectively increased and decreased by T cell activation in 1% O2 (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis showing decreased c-Myc protein levels in 1% O2 activated T cells, as shown in Figure 5B, and by citation to Wang et al., 2011.

claim: 1% O2 culture and PHD inhibition both decrease mTOR activation, as assessed by reduced phosphorylation of mTOR (Ser2448) and S6 Ribosomal Protein (Ser235/236).
source: Moreover, 1% O2 culture and PHD inhibition both decreased mTOR activation, as assessed by the reduction in phosphorylation of mTOR (Ser2448) and its target S6 Ribosomal Protein (Ser235/236) (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis of phospho-mTOR and phospho-S6 shown in Figure 5C.

claim: T cell activation in low oxygen increases the production of IL-2 when compared to cells activated in ambient oxygen.
source: T cell activation in low oxygen increased the production of IL-2 when compared to cells activated in ambient oxygen (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing increased IL-2 levels in supernatants of 1% O2 activated T cells, as shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The increase in IL-2 production following 24 hr of T cell activation in hypoxia is accompanied by an increase in STAT5 phosphorylation (Y694) and in the expression of IL-2 receptor subunit CD25.
source: In fact, we observed that the increase in IL-2 production following 24 hr of T cell activation in hypoxia was accompanied by an increase in STAT5 phosphorylation (Y694) and in the expression of IL-2 receptor subunit CD25 (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis of pSTAT5 and CD25 shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Expression of Blimp-1 is decreased in CD8+ T cells following 24 hr of activation in 1% O2.
source: In contrast with pSTAT5 and CD25, expression of Blimp-1 was decreased in CD8+ T cells following 24 hr of activation in 1% O2 (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis of Blimp-1 shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Conditioning to 1% O2 exclusively during the first 24 hr of activation of OT-I cells results in lower baseline intracellular calcium levels on day 7.
source: We found that conditioning to 1% O2 exclusively during the first 24 hr of activation of OT-I cells resulted in lower baseline intracellular calcium levels on day 7 when compared to cells continuously cultured in ambient oxygen.
evidence: Supported by single-cell calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Restimulation with SIINFEKL at day 7 induces a much higher store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) in cells conditioned to 1% O2 for the first 24 hr of activation.
source: However, restimulation with SIINFEKL at day 7 induced a much higher store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) in the cells conditioned to 1% O2 (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by single-cell calcium imaging data showing increased calcium response to SIINFEKL in 1% 1d cells, as shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A single day of 1% O2 conditioning followed by 6 d of culture in 21% enhances the killing capacity of both HER2- and CD19-CAR-T cells.
source: However, a single day of 1% O2 conditioning followed by 6 d of culture in 21% enhanced the killing capacity of both HER2- and CD19-CAR-T cells, with a significantly increased secretion of IFN-γ (Figure 6B and C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: Supported by in vitro cytotoxicity assay data showing lower EC50 values and increased IFN-γ secretion for 1% 1d CAR-T cells, as shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: A single day of 1% O2 conditioning of HER2-CAR-T cells significantly enhances their immunotherapeutic function against SKOV3 tumours, as shown by decreased tumour growth rates and increased animal survival.
source: A single day of 1% O2 conditioning of HER2-CAR-T cells significantly enhanced their immunotherapeutic function against SKOV3 tumours, as shown by significantly decreased tumour growth rates, and by increased animal survival, relative to animals receiving 21% O2-treated CAR-T cells (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: Supported by tumour growth measurements and survival analysis shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: OT-I cells activated for 1 d at 1% O2 and expanded for 6 d in ambient oxygen show a striking increase in tumour infiltration compared to 21% controls.
source: Following ACT into tumour-bearing hosts, we found a striking increase of OT-I infiltration in the 1% 1 d group relative to the 21% controls, both per gram of tumour and per million CD45+ cells (Figure 6J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1O).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis of tumour-infiltrated lymphocytes shown in Figure 6J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1O.

claim: Longer exposure to 1% O2 can hinder antitumour T cell function.
source: We additionally found that longer exposure to 1% O2 could hinder antitumour T cell function (Figure 6—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: Supported by cytotoxicity assay data showing impaired function with prolonged 1% O2 exposure, as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1L.

claim: Oxygen tensions during activation can act to permanently shift T cell function.
source: These findings, which are summarised in Figure 7, indicate that oxygen tensions during activation can act to permanently shift T cell function and that the hypoxic response can be harnessed to improve T cell-based immunotherapeutic strategies.
evidence: Inferred from the persistent effects of short-term low oxygen conditioning on T cell differentiation, metabolism, and function observed throughout the study.

claim: The hypoxic response can be harnessed to improve T cell-based immunotherapeutic strategies.
source: These findings, which are summarised in Figure 7, indicate that oxygen tensions during activation can act to permanently shift T cell function and that the hypoxic response can be harnessed to improve T cell-based immunotherapeutic strategies.
evidence: Inferred from the improved antitumour efficacy of T cells conditioned to low oxygen during activation, as demonstrated in multiple in vivo experiments.

claim: Tumour hypoxia recruits immunosuppressive regulatory T cells, which can inhibit CD8+ T cell function.
source: For example, tumour hypoxia recruits immunosuppressive regulatory T cells, which can inhibit CD8+ T cell function (Facciabene et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Facciabene et al., 2011.

claim: Hypoxia decreases expression of MHC class I molecules in tumour cells, which hampers T cell priming and cytotoxic function.
source: Hypoxia is also known to decrease expression of MHC class I molecules in tumour cells themselves, which in turn hampers T cell priming and cytotoxic function (Sethumadhavan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sethumadhavan et al., 2017.

claim: Tumour hypoxia can have direct inhibitory effects on CD8+ T cells by increasing the expression of checkpoint inhibitor receptors.
source: Tumour hypoxia can also have direct inhibitory effects on CD8+ T cells by increasing the expression of checkpoint inhibitor receptors (Bannoud et al., 2021; Noman et al., 2015) and cause mitochondrial dysfunction (Liu et al., 2020; Scharping et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bannoud et al., 2021 and Noman et al., 2015.

claim: Tumour hypoxia can cause mitochondrial dysfunction in CD8+ T cells.
source: Tumour hypoxia can also have direct inhibitory effects on CD8+ T cells by increasing the expression of checkpoint inhibitor receptors (Bannoud et al., 2021; Noman et al., 2015) and cause mitochondrial dysfunction (Liu et al., 2020; Scharping et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 2020 and Scharping et al., 2021.

claim: CD8+ T cells are typically cultured at atmospheric sea-level O2 conditions (approximately 20.5%) in preclinical studies and clinical manufacturing.
source: In both preclinical studies and clinical manufacturing, CD8+ T cells are typically cultured at atmospheric sea-level O2 conditions (approximately 20.5%); however, reports have shown that physiologically relevant oxygen tensions (corresponding to 1–5% O2) can profoundly shift T cell differentiation and function (Atkuri et al., 2007; Caldwell et al., 2001; Gropper et al., 2017; Larbi et al., 2010; Loeffler et al., 1990; Naldini et al., 1997; Palazon et al., 2017; Ross et al., 2021; Veliça et al., 2021).
evidence: Stated as established practice in the field.

claim: Physiologically relevant oxygen tensions (1–5% O2) can profoundly shift T cell differentiation and function.
source: In both preclinical studies and clinical manufacturing, CD8+ T cells are typically cultured at atmospheric sea-level O2 conditions (approximately 20.5%); however, reports have shown that physiologically relevant oxygen tensions (corresponding to 1–5% O2) can profoundly shift T cell differentiation and function (Atkuri et al., 2007; Caldwell et al., 2001; Gropper et al., 2017; Larbi et al., 2010; Loeffler et al., 1990; Naldini et al., 1997; Palazon et al., 2017; Ross et al., 2021; Veliça et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Lower oxygen levels alter CD8+ T cell effector differentiation in a process that requires hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs).
source: Lower oxygen levels alter CD8+ T cell effector differentiation in a process that requires hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs), the key transcriptional regulators of cellular responses to low oxygen (Finlay et al., 2012; Palazon et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Finlay et al., 2012 and Palazon et al., 2017.

claim: Culturing CD8+ T cells ex vivo at 1% O2 dramatically reduces T cell proliferation but increases antitumour activity upon transfer into tumour-bearing mice.
source: Culturing CD8+ T cells ex vivo at 1% O2 has been found to dramatically reduce T cell proliferation, but increase antitumour activity, upon transfer into tumour-bearing mice (Gropper et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gropper et al., 2017.

claim: 24 hr of low oxygen levels during initial CD8+ T cell priming is sufficient to enhance antitumour cytotoxicity in a preclinical model, even when CAR-T cells are subsequently cultured under high oxygen tensions prior to adoptive transfer.
source: We found that in a protocol of CAR-T cell generation, 24 hr of low oxygen levels during initial CD8+ T cell priming is sufficient to enhance antitumour cytotoxicity in a preclinical model. This is the case even when CAR-T cells are subsequently cultured under high oxygen tensions prior to adoptive transfer.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from CAR-T cell studies showing improved antitumour efficacy with 1 day of 1% O2 conditioning.

claim: Only a controlled or temporary increase in HIF signalling is able to consistently improve cytotoxic function of T cells.
source: Increased hypoxia-inducible transcription factor (HIF) expression was able to alter T cell fate in a similar manner to exposure to low oxygen tensions; however, only a controlled or temporary increase in HIF signalling was able to consistently improve cytotoxic function of T cells.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of short-term versus long-term HIF modulation on T cell function observed throughout the study.

claim: Oxygenation levels during and immediately after T cell activation play an essential role in regulating T cell function.
source: These data show that oxygenation levels during and immediately after T cell activation play an essential role in regulating T cell function.
evidence: Inferred from the persistent effects of oxygen levels during activation on T cell differentiation, metabolism, and function observed throughout the study.
